content.comment_body: I plan to use 4 [product_name] units in a project, all connected to an HMI. I have attached a sketch and program in a PDF. Is it possible to accomplish this setup with [product_name] and an HMI? Can I also reset and silence alarms from the HMI?

There are several options. If you only need to acknowledge two alarms across the four [product_name] devices, you can send signals to just one [product_name] from the HMI, which can forward the acknowledgment bits to the other three using the VM range. Alternatively, you may choose an HMI capable of managing at least four connections and send the acknowledgment bits directly from the HMI to each [product_name] using the VM range.
Why did you change your username? This is causing some confusion.
I prefer not to have plc in my username.
You chose the username with plc yourself. No one else did.
I changed my mind.
I changed my mind, and also my avatar.
I changed my mind and also my avatar. Good point.
New username and new avatar—looks nice. Any updates on your project, though? Have you solved your issue?

I'm now considering a [version_no] controller. I emailed the local [company_name] contact for help, and I also received a support email from [company_name]. The response states: Dear Sir/Madam, You can definitely connect multiple [product_name] controllers to an HMI panel. However, certain factors may restrict this: - Connection type, such as PPI/MPI/Ethernet - HMI panel series and connection limits - Software used for configuration (e.g., Protool or [product_name]) I need to choose between [product_name] and [version_no]. While [product_name] is more budget-friendly, connecting multiple [product_name] units and the HMI may be challenging. I'm working on the HMI design and programming with [product_name] software for [version_no].
I previously explained that [product_name] does not support PPI or MPI. The [article_no] standard only supports Ethernet TCP/IP, and since version FS04, also Modbus TCP/IP.

I've completed the [product_name] program for this project (see attachment). Each [product_name] has 5 inputs, with 4 units making a total of 20 inputs. Four signals will be sent from the HMI to [product_name]: Test lamp, Accept, Alarm Mute, and Reset Alarm. Program and sketch attached—I need guidance on VM mapping, as I haven't used it before.
Is the program identical on every [product_name]?
Yes, it is.
Does it matter if the program is the same, but the [product_name] devices themselves differ?

Please clarify the differences. Are you using different types of [product_name] like [article_no] standard and FS04? If so, specify which kind each unit is. For example: [product_name] 1 = [article_no] standard, [product_name] 2 = FS04, etc.
[product_name] 1 = [article_no] standard [product_name] 2 = [article_no] standard [product_name] 3 = [article_no] standard [product_name] 4 = [article_no] standard
I don't understand your description. Referring to your previous post, what are the actual differences?
I meant even though the program is the same, there are four [product_name] devices involved.

I've prepared a network project for you using four [product_name] [article_no] standard units, each running the same logic. The only program differences are the command rankings from the HMI. You’ll need to specify IP addresses for each [product_name] and the HMI. In [product_name] software, connect to [product_name] 1; the other three receive commands relayed by [product_name] 1. You'll need to set operands for the HMI buttons accordingly.

Thank you for your effort. I've reviewed the connections and program changes, so the HMI now communicates with [product_name] 1, which passes commands to the rest. I've also created an HMI program using [product_name] V13 for an HMI device, but I can't figure out how to link [product_name] to it, or connect the output to the HMI's LED circle.
I can see that HMI inputs reach the [product_name], but I still need to map the outputs (q2–q6) between each [product_name] (1, 2, 3, 4) and the HMI.
I found the [product_name] driver under connections.

Based on my understanding, I need to assign q2–q6 from [product_name] 4 to [product_name] 1, q2–q6 from [product_name] 3 to [product_name] 1, and q2–q6 from [product_name] 2 to [product_name] 1. This way, all 20 inputs are mapped in [product_name] 1, ready to be tagged to the HMI LEDs.
Here is the updated version with outputs mapped to the HMI via [product_name] 1.

Hi [user_name], I'm considering an update: I want the HMI signals (Accept, Mute, Reset, Lamp Test) to be shared among all four [product_name] units. If I reset, it will apply to all four with one signal. Please review my modification.

Is it possible to use just one operand set for all units? [product_name] 1, [product_name] 2, [product_name] 3, [product_name] 4 Lamp Test = DB1.DBX 0.0 Accept = DB1.DBX 0.1 Alarm Mute = DB1.DBX 0.2 Reset Alarm = DB1.DBX 0.3
I can tag these individually to the HMI. Please check the attached screenshot.
Here is the modified version with just four HMI signals for all [product_name] devices. And yes, you can directly use the V addresses of the [product_name] units with the HMI variable settings.

Thanks. In this setup, everything depends on [product_name] 1. If it needs to be turned off for maintenance (e.g., in engine panel 1), the system stops working because communication is lost. So, I'm thinking of adding a fifth unit as a communication hub. This fifth unit won't use any inputs/outputs and can be placed in a safe location like the control room, with the other four units on their respective engine locations.

No offense, but you're not presenting a clear concept. You're refining your requirements gradually and seem to lack some foundational knowledge. Now you're mentioning a fifth [product_name] unit. If [product_name] 1 fails, the others can’t operate. What will you do if the HMI fails? I also asked earlier which HMI model you plan to use, but you haven't specified—only mentioning a basic panel. Without clear details, it's hard to provide meaningful suggestions.

Yes, I'm a beginner, but this is a valuable learning experience. I've come to realize how important planning and considering all options is. Initially, I wasn't aware that mapping inputs and outputs only to one [product_name] is so critical for connecting multiple units.

You should first clarify your objectives, focusing on hardware selection and whether the software supports your needs. If you need more than four [product_name] units, select a panel that manages more than four connections. You can connect each unit independently with the right data. If you don’t want ‘chief’ unit–mediated data exchange, use individual communication for each unit. Up to four connections are possible with a [company_name] basic panel; more units require another panel. Forums can't serve as instant training courses.
The HMI connection always involves one [product_name] communicating with the HMI, acting as the chief. Since the HMI sees a single connection, it should work fine with a [company_name] HMI panel.

A [company_name] basic panel can manage up to four connections. With just an Ethernet cable, the HMI can establish up to four separate connections—one per [product_name] unit. In this scenario, you wouldn't need a 'boss' unit.

But we’re using a boss [product_name] unit, and if a fifth is added, it becomes the boss. More than four shouldn't be a problem, as long as we use a boss unit—since there's just one actual connection, right?

I'm still unclear about your plan. Sometimes you prefer distributed, sometimes centralized connections. If you want the HMI to communicate only through a 'boss' [product_name], it must handle everything. If the 'boss' fails, communication is lost. Alternatively, a [company_name] comfort panel can support up to eight connections.

I want the boss [product_name] to be a dedicated fifth unit—not 1, 2, 3, or 4—so maintenance on 1 through 4 doesn't disrupt the system. The first four units will be in the engine room, while the fifth (boss) will be in the control room, connected via Ethernet.
So proceed with that design. Is there another issue you're facing now? I’ve created a template for you—feel free to use it.
Here is the updated version with a 'boss' [product_name] and four other units.
A new question by [user_name] has been moved to a separate thread titled 'Can use two HMI if using a [version_no] CPU and 4 [product_name] units.' Best regards [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: The user is exploring the possibility and challenges of linking four [product_name] units to a single HMI for remote alarm control. Forum responses highlight key dependencies such as HMI type, connection limits, and software compatibility. As complexity emerges—particularly with technical hurdles and architectural constraints—the user considers moving to a [version_no] controller for better scalability and ease of integration. The discussion reflects technical uncertainty and the need for a solution well-matched to project demands.
analysis.user_expectations: The user seeks seamless integration of several [product_name] units with an HMI and easy remote handling of alarm functions, hoping for minimal technical complications in achieving these goals.
feature_keywords: alarm reset and silence via HMI
